title: DSCR vs. Conventional Financing: Which Path Fits Your Deal

slides.title: Compare both loans on five-year cost, pick one to chase, and keep the other live
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.7. DSCR vs. Conventional Financing: Which Path Fits Your Deal
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, or lending advice. The lender makes the eligibility call.
slides.notes:
In PA.6 we priced one financing path. Now we put two side by side.

By the end you can lay a DSCR quote and a conventional quote side by side. Same house, same buyer. You'll see the difference in cash to close, monthly payment, five-year cost, paperwork, and flexibility. Then you'll use a decision tree to pick which lender to call first.

One thing up front. The decision tree orders your phone calls. It doesn't decide whether you qualify. The lender makes that call, every time.

We stay with Cedar Ridge. Maya and Chris, $385,000, 25% down. Both quotes are hypothetical, and every Cedar Ridge figure is an assumption from our running Cedar Ridge example.

slides.title: A DSCR loan is sized on the property; a conventional loan is sized on your household

left.head: DSCR
left.note: Debt service coverage ratio: the property's income divided by its loan payment (PA.6)
items: Shorter paperwork
Often allows an LLC on title
Usually a higher rate and cost

right.head: Conventional
right.note: Mostly your documented income, debts, credit, and assets
items: Full income and asset documents
Ask about an LLC; often personal names
Usually lower cost for strong borrowers

slides.notes:
A DSCR loan sizes the loan mostly on the property's income. DSCR stands for debt service coverage ratio. It's the property's income divided by its loan payment. A ratio of 1.0 means the income just covers the payment. PA.6 covers how lenders calculate it.

A conventional loan sizes it mostly on you: your documented income, your existing debts, your credit, and your assets. The property still matters, but your household is the main borrower.

That one difference changes almost everything else. It changes which documents you gather and how long underwriting takes. It changes whether you can close in an LLC. And it changes what happens to your borrowing capacity for the next property.

Every line on this slide says "usually" or "often" for a reason. These are typical patterns, and they vary by lender. Confirm each one with the actual lender you're talking to.

slides.title: On Cedar Ridge, the conventional quote wins on every line
slides.text: A $385,000 house, $288,750 loan, 25% down. DSCR: 7.25%, 1 point (1% of the loan). Conventional: 6.875%, no points.
slides.caption: PITIA = principal, interest, taxes, insurance, dues. Total cash in adds $32,000 of furnishing. Reserves not included. Cash flow: next slide.
slides.notes:
Here's the side-by-side for Cedar Ridge, a $385,000 house. Both quotes are hypothetical. DSCR at 7.25% with one point, which means 1% of the loan paid at closing. Conventional at 6.875% with no points. Both 30-year fixed, both 25% down, both a $288,750 loan. I hold the down payment equal so the comparison is fair.

Walk down the rows. P&I is principal and interest. PITIA adds taxes, insurance, and association dues, so it's the full payment. The conventional payment is $1,897 against $1,970. Closing costs are $11,550 against $14,438, because there's no point. Cash to close is $107,800 against $110,688. Total cash in adds the $32,000 furnishing budget. Principal paid in year one is higher on conventional too. Cash-on-cash, first-year cash flow divided by total cash in, is 4.6% against 3.9%.

The conventional quote wins on every line.

One thing this table leaves out is reserves. Either lender may require months of PITIA on top of cash to close. Ask both.

slides.title: Both loans lose money in the weak case and in the 18% co-host case
slides.caption: Base: $300 ADR (average nightly rate), 58% occupancy. Weak: $265 ADR, 50% occupancy. Annual cash flow = NOI minus principal and interest; taxes and insurance are already inside NOI. All figures are assumptions from the Cedar Ridge example.
slides.notes:
Here's the part that matters most. Look at the cash flow lines. Green is money in. Red is a loss.

The base case assumes a $300 average nightly rate, which is ADR, and 58% occupancy, the share of nights booked. There, DSCR leaves $5,572 a year and conventional leaves $6,446. Conventional is better by $874.

Now the weak case, where ADR drops to $265 and occupancy to 50%. DSCR loses $5,475 a year. Conventional loses $4,601. Both lose money.

Now say Maya and Chris hand the house to a full-service co-host at 18% in the base case. Both loans go negative: minus $7,798 on DSCR, minus $6,924 on conventional. If you plan to use a co-host, run that case before you buy. OP.7 covers the staffing choice.

Financing changes the size of the loss. It doesn't change the house. Here the base case works on both loans. The weak case and the co-host case don't work on either. Keep that in mind when we set the offer ceiling in PA.8.

slides.title: A conventional lender weighs four things about you, under the loan buyer's rules
columns: What Fannie Mae's Selling Guide says (one public example)
rows: 36% max for manual underwriting (a person applying the rules by hand); up to 45% with credit score and reserves; 50% through Desktop Underwriter (DU), the automated system (B3-6-02).
W-2s, tax returns, pay stubs. Self-employment needs more. The lender decides what counts.

Principal residence, second home, or investment (B2-1.1-01). Investment loans carry an extra price adjustment (LLPA). One-unit investment purchase: up to 85% LTV (loan-to-value), so at least 15% down.
Reserves rise with the number of financed properties when the new loan is a second home or investment (B3-4.1-01, B2-2-03).
slides.caption: Lenders sell many loans to buyers like Fannie Mae, which set the rules. Your loan may follow Fannie Mae, another loan buyer's guide, or the lender's own portfolio rules. Ask which guide applies.
slides.notes:
On a conventional loan, the lender underwrites your household. I'm using Fannie Mae's Selling Guide as the example because it's public. Lenders sell many loans to buyers like Fannie Mae, and the loan buyer sets the rules. So your loan may follow Fannie Mae, another loan buyer's guide, or the lender's own rules. Ask which one.

Four things carry most of the weight. First, debt-to-income: your monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income. Fannie Mae sets 36% for manual underwriting, where a person applies the rules by hand. It allows up to 45% with the right credit score and reserves, and 50% through its automated system, Desktop Underwriter.

Second, documented income. Third, occupancy type. Investment loans carry an extra price adjustment. A one-unit investment purchase can go up to 85% loan-to-value, so at least 15% down.

Fourth, reserves and your other properties. Maya and Chris would have two financed properties: their home and Cedar Ridge. Personal use is one of the things that separates a second home from an investment property. So don't guess the occupancy type from their 10 personal-use days. Tell the lender the real plan and let it classify.

slides.title: With zero STR income counted, Maya and Chris's DTI would be about 35.6%

lines.label: Cedar Ridge conventional PITIA, no rental income → monthly debts $5,484

slides.side:
That's 0.4 points under the 36% manual limit, and well under 45% and 50%.

Through DU, the STR income question may not decide their loan. On a manual file, there's almost no room, so they also take a Branch C step.

side_box.label: Screening only
side_box.text: The lender runs the real DTI on your actual debts, credit, reserves, and underwriting system.

slides.notes:
Here's a rough DTI check. It's an illustration. The lender runs the real one.

Maya and Chris earn $185,000 a year combined. That's from the Cedar Ridge example. Monthly, that's $15,417.

I need two numbers the example doesn't give, so I've made them up and marked them. Say their home payment is $2,400 a month and car and card payments are $600. That's $3,000 of monthly debts. Divide by $15,417 and their DTI today is 19.5%.

Now add the full Cedar Ridge conventional PITIA of $2,484, and count zero rental income. Monthly debts become $5,484. Divide by $15,417 and DTI goes to 35.6%.

That sits just under the 36% limit for manual underwriting, even if the lender gives the STR no income credit at all. It's well under the 45% and 50% limits.

Why does this matter? Through Desktop Underwriter, or with the credit and reserves for 45%, the STR income question may not decide their loan. On a manual file, 35.6% leaves only 0.4 points of room. That's what "near the limit" means in the decision tree. So Maya and Chris also take one Branch C step.

slides.title: Fannie Mae added a short-term rental income section in September 2026
slides.keyline: "Conventional loans can't use Airbnb income" is out of date. Whether the new section fits your deal is the lender's call.

nodes.d: Adds B3-3.8-03, Rental Income from the Subject Property: Short-Term Rental
Fannie Mae encourages lenders to apply it immediately
For all loans with application dates on or after this date

box.label: Not confirmed yet
box.text: Not confirmed for this lesson: exact eligibility, occupancy types, purchase vs. refinance, history, and documents. Get them from your lender in writing.

slides.notes:
You'll hear people say conventional loans can't use Airbnb income. Don't repeat that. It's out of date.

On September 2, 2026, Fannie Mae published Announcement SEL-2026-08. It restructured the rental income chapter and added a section called B3-3.8-03, Rental Income from the Subject Property: Short-Term Rental. The announcement says it introduces new requirements for using STR income, including alternative documentation options.

On timing, as of September 2026: lenders are encouraged to adopt it immediately. They must apply it to loans with application dates on or after November 1, 2026. So for an application before November 1, ask your loan officer directly whether they've adopted it. From November 1 on, the question is whether your transaction fits.

I need to be straight with you. The exact conditions in the new section were not confirmed for this lesson. That includes eligibility, occupancy types, purchase or refinance, operating history, and documents. Those conditions decide whether Cedar Ridge qualifies. Get them from your lender in writing.

slides.title: Occupancy type and the new section's fit decide whether STR income counts
items: If the lender confirms the transaction fits B3-3.8-03, it may count documented STR income under that section's rules.
If the property is classified as a second home, rental income generally can't be used to qualify (B3-3.8-01).
If the transaction doesn't fit the section, the lender may still approve on W-2 income alone. Maya and Chris's DTI suggests that's possible.

box.label: Confirm with
box.text: The lender: whether the loan follows Fannie Mae's guide, whether B3-3.8-03 applies to this transaction and application date, and which STR documents it will accept.

slides.notes:
The exact conditions weren't confirmed for this lesson, so here's the conditional version.

If the lender confirms that Cedar Ridge's transaction fits B3-3.8-03, it may count documented STR income under that section's calculation rules.

What if the lender classifies the property as a second home? Fannie Mae's general rental income section says second-home rental income generally can't be used to qualify. It lists narrow exceptions.

If the transaction doesn't fit the new section at all, the lender may still approve the loan on W-2 income alone. The DTI check we just did suggests that's possible for Maya and Chris.

So your job on the first call is to ask three things. Does this loan follow Fannie Mae's guide? Does B3-3.8-03 apply to my transaction and my application date? And exactly which STR documents will you accept? Get the answers in writing.

slides.title: Over five years, the DSCR loan costs Maya and Chris about $8,342 more
slides.caption: Both loans run for 60 months from the two Cedar Ridge quotes. $4,374 more in payments plus $1,080 more owed at payoff equals the $5,454 of extra interest. Don't count the $1,080 twice.
slides.notes:
The monthly payments differ by $73. That looks small. Over five years it adds up, and the points add more on day one.

I ran both loans for 60 months from the two Cedar Ridge quotes. The DSCR loan costs $2,888 in points at closing. It pays $5,454 more in interest. Add those and it costs Maya and Chris about $8,342 more over five years.

They'd also owe $1,080 more at the end, because less of each DSCR payment went to principal. That isn't an extra cost on top. $4,374 more in payments plus $1,080 more owed at payoff equals the $5,454 of extra interest. Don't count it twice.

Same warning for cash flow. Over five years the base-case gap is about $4,370. That's the same payment difference seen from the operating side. Don't add it to the $8,342.

Build this table for your own deal, because a DSCR term sheet may not show an APR. Five-year interest plus points plus closing costs is the fairest single number you have.

slides.title: A 5-4-3-2-1 penalty would add $2,725 if the DSCR loan is paid off at the year-five sale
slides.side:
5-4-3-2-1 means 5% of the balance in year 1, stepping down to 1% in year 5.

This is on top of the $8,342: about $11,067 in total if the penalty applies.

With a 3-2-1 schedule (assumption), there'd be no penalty at year five. Ask the conventional lender in writing whether any penalty applies.
slides.notes:
Now add the exit. In the Cedar Ridge example, Maya and Chris sell at the end of year five.

Say the DSCR loan has a 5-4-3-2-1 step-down penalty. That's 5% of the balance if you pay off in year one and 4% in year two. It steps down to 1% in year five. That's an example structure, not a standard.

A payoff in month 60 is still in year five, so the penalty is 1% of $272,519. That's $2,725. And it's on top of the $8,342, so about $11,067 in total if this penalty applies.

With a 3-2-1 schedule, 3% in year one down to 1% in year three, there'd be no penalty at year five. So the schedule matters as much as the rate. Ask the conventional lender to confirm in writing whether any prepayment penalty applies to its loan too.

slides.title: Compare the same eight lines on each written quote, dated the same day
items: Interest rate, whether it's locked, and for how long
APR where shown (rate plus points and certain charges)
Points and lender credits, in dollars
Estimated cash to close
Monthly P&I and full monthly PITIA
Reserves required after closing, in dollars
Prepayment penalty, year by year
Refinance terms: wait period, max cash-out, STR income method

box.label: Term sheet or Loan Estimate
box.text: Rental credit you won't occupy is business-purpose credit (Reg Z, § 1026.3), so a lender may send a term sheet. Ask for every rate, fee, and penalty in the same layout.

slides.notes:
The CFPB's guide to comparing loan offers tells you to request several Loan Estimates and focus on the fees that vary by lender. It also warns that rates change daily. So get both quotes on the same day if you can.

Compare these eight lines. The APR matters because, as the CFPB explains, it includes the rate plus points and certain other charges. Estimated cash to close includes your down payment and closing costs, minus your deposit and any seller credits.

The last line is the one people forget: what the lender will require at refinance. How long you must own the property first, which lenders call seasoning. How much cash you can pull out on a cash-out refinance, where the new loan is larger and you take the difference. And how it will count STR income then.

One wrinkle. Federal rules treat credit to buy a rental you won't occupy as business-purpose credit. So a lender may not have to give you a Loan Estimate. Some will anyway. Others send a term sheet, a short summary of the rate, fees, and terms. Either way, get every rate, fee, and penalty in writing, in the same layout.

slides.title: Each route gives and takes on paperwork, title, and the next loan, so confirm every line
rows: Mostly yours, plus eligible rental income
Shorter: no tax returns at Kiavi, per its site
Not used to qualify this loan
A future conventional lender counts it under its own rules
Also counted under the future lender's rules
slides.caption: Both columns vary by lender. Future lenders apply rules like Fannie Mae's B3-6-06 on other real estate owned.
slides.notes:
Price isn't the only difference. Here's what each route tends to give and take. Every line varies by lender, so confirm it with the actual lender.

The row I want you to notice is "effect on the next loan." Some buyers assume a DSCR loan keeps the property off their record. It doesn't work that way. A future conventional lender will count Cedar Ridge under its own rules. Fannie Mae's rules on other real estate owned, section B3-6-06, govern how a future conventional lender counts it.

That matters when Maya and Chris apply for property two. So keep clean records from day one. Booking statements. The Schedule E your CPA files, the tax-return form that reports rental income and expenses. The loan payment history.

OP.11 picks up the refinance and property two. For now, just start the folder.

slides.title: First rental on W-2 income: get the conventional quote first and keep DSCR live

gates.q: Is your DTI, with the full new payment and no rental income, under the limit with room to spare?
gates.sub: Yes → get a conventional quote first.
gates.no: No or close → also run Branch C

gates.q: Will the lender classify the property as an investment property?
gates.no: Ask what that means for rental income and occupancy

gates.q: Can you close the way you need to (LLC now, if required) on the conventional loan?
Is the conventional approval in writing?
gates.no: Keep the DSCR quote live as backup

slides.end: The tree orders your calls. The lender makes the eligibility decision.
slides.notes:
Here's the decision tree. Use it to decide which lender to call first. It orders your calls. The lender makes the actual eligibility decision.

Branch A is buying your first rental with documented W-2 income. That's Maya and Chris.

Step one: is your DTI, with the full new payment and no rental income, under the lender's limit with some room to spare? If yes, get a conventional quote first. If you're over the limit, or within a point or two of it, also follow Branch C.

Step two: will the lender classify it as an investment property? If yes, keep going. If not, ask what that means for rental income and occupancy rules.

Step three: can you close the way you need to on the conventional loan, in an LLC now if you need one? If yes, keep going. If no, get a DSCR quote.

Step four: is the conventional approval in writing? Until it is, keep a DSCR quote live as your backup. Deals stall in underwriting. A live backup means you don't lose the house when one does.

slides.eyebrow: Decision tree · Branches B and C
slides.title: A refinance and a thin-income file each follow their own branch of the tree

left.head: Branch B: refinance an STR you own
items: 12+ months of statements and a filed Schedule E? Ask if B3-3.8-03 or the lender's rules count it.
Price your current prepayment penalty in dollars first.
Does weak-case cash flow still meet the minimum you set for yourself after the refinance?
Compare conventional and DSCR on the same day, same amount.

right.head: Branch C: complex or thin income
right.note: Self-employed with short history, job changes, big write-offs, or DTI over or near the limit
items: Ask a conventional lender to pre-underwrite your income first.
If your income won't carry it, DSCR may fit. Plan the higher cost in PA.8.
Check weak-case cash flow on DSCR pricing. DSCR removes the income test, not the risk.

slides.notes:
Two more branches.

Branch B is a refinance of an STR you already own. Do you have 12 months or more of platform statements and a filed Schedule E? Ask the conventional lender whether B3-3.8-03 or its own rules would count that income. Does your current loan have a prepayment penalty? Price it in dollars before you compare anything. Then check the weak case. If the refinance pushes weak-case cash flow below the minimum you set for yourself, the refinance is making the property riskier. PA.8 walks through setting that rule. And compare both loan types on the same day for the same amount.

Branch C is for complex or thin income documentation. Self-employed with a short history, recent job changes, large write-offs, or DTI over or within a point or two of the limit. Don't assume you won't qualify. Ask a conventional lender to pre-underwrite your income first. If your income truly won't carry the payment, a DSCR loan may fit. Just remember: DSCR removes the income test. It doesn't remove the risk.

slides.title: Maya and Chris pursue conventional first but set their offer on the DSCR numbers

nodes.d: Just under 36%, thin margin. Conventional first; ask for a pre-underwrite.
About 10 personal days a year. Assume investment.
PA.10 entity work isn't done yet
Over five years, plus up to $2,725 more with a DSCR penalty. $2,888 less at closing.

box.label: Their written decision
box.text: Pursue conventional first. Keep DSCR as the backup. Use the DSCR numbers in PA.8 until the conventional approval is in writing.

slides.notes:
Let's run Cedar Ridge through Branch A.

Step one: DTI with the full conventional PITIA and no STR income is 35.6%. That's well under the higher limits, so conventional quote first. On a manual file, though, it's only 0.4 points under 36%. So they also ask the lender for a pre-underwrite before relying on it.

Step two: occupancy. They plan about 10 personal-use days a year and rent the rest. They tell the lender that plan and ask for the classification in writing. This lesson assumes investment property.

Step three: LLC. They'd like liability separation, but the lender's rules and the PA.10 entity work aren't done yet. They ask and write down the answer.

Step four: cost. Conventional saves $2,888 at closing and about $8,342 over five years. Add up to $2,725 more if the DSCR loan carries that penalty. Base-case cash flow is $874 a year better.

Step five: they keep the DSCR quote live. If underwriting stalls, they switch without losing the house.

They set the offer on the DSCR numbers. You set your ceiling on the more expensive loan you might end up with.

slides.title: Fill one column per written quote, then answer four one-line questions
rows: Lender, date, rate / APR, points and credits ($)
Cash to close, reserves, monthly P&I / PITIA ($)
Prepayment penalty by year; refinance terms
Occupancy type assigned; rental income counted?
Your DTI per the lender; title in names or LLC?
Base-case and weak-case annual cash flow
slides.notes:
Here's your exercise. The full table in the lesson has 16 lines. I've grouped them here so you see the shape. Fill in one column per written quote. Use your PA.6 worksheet for the DSCR side, and your NOI from Sam's PA.4 package for the cash flow lines.

No property or quotes yet? Practice with Cedar Ridge. Put the DSCR numbers in Quote 1 and the conventional numbers in Quote 2.

For five-year interest on your own quotes, ask each lender for an amortization schedule. That's the month-by-month split of each payment into interest and principal. Add up the interest for months 1 to 60.

Don't skip the occupancy line. The lender assigns it, not you, and it decides whether rental income counts at all.

Then answer four questions in one line each. Which branch are you on? Which quote costs less over your expected hold? Which keeps weak-case cash flow closer to breakeven? And what would make you switch to the backup? Write that trigger down before you need it.

box.label: Then answer in one line each
box.text:
1. Your branch? 2. Cheaper over your hold? 3. Closer to weak-case breakeven? 4. Your switch trigger?

No quotes yet? Practice with Cedar Ridge: DSCR in Quote 1, conventional in Quote 2 (slides 3 and 9).

slides.title: Each lender confirms its own eligibility; your CPA and attorney cover records and title
rows: Occupancy classification, whether the loan follows Fannie Mae's guide, whether B3-3.8-03 applies to this transaction and date, your DTI, reserves for all financed properties, and whether an LLC can hold title.
The PA.6 question list, especially the prepayment schedule and maximum loan.
How you'll document STR income on your return so a future lender can use it, and how the points you pay are treated on your taxes.
What signing in personal names versus an LLC means for liability and title (PA.10).
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

The conventional lender has the longest list. The occupancy classification. Whether the loan follows Fannie Mae's guide. Whether B3-3.8-03 applies to your transaction and your application date. Your DTI as they calculate it. The reserves they need across all your financed properties. And whether an LLC can hold title.

The DSCR lender confirms everything on the PA.6 question list. The two that matter most here are the prepayment schedule and the maximum loan.

Your CPA confirms how you'll document STR income on your tax return so a future lender can actually use it. That's the property-two problem, and it starts with this year's return. The CPA also confirms how the points you pay are treated on your taxes.

Your attorney confirms what signing in personal names versus an LLC means for liability and title. PA.10 covers that decision in full.

slides.next: Next: PA.8 Offer Strategy & Negotiation for Investment Property. Bring your comparison table and Sam's PA.4 package.
slides.notes:
Four things this week.

First, run your own screening DTI. Full new PITIA, zero rental income. It tells you which branch you're on.

Second, request both quotes on the same day, for the same address and the same loan amount.

Third, ask the conventional lender two questions in writing: how it classifies the occupancy, and whether B3-3.8-03 applies to your transaction and date.

Fourth, build the five-year cost table and write down four things: your branch, your first call, your backup, and what would make you switch.

You've picked a financing route and a backup. PA.8 uses the more expensive of the two quotes to set Maya and Chris's walk-away price before they negotiate. Bring your comparison table and Sam's PA.4 underwriting package.

slides.notes:
Here are the main sources.

The conventional rules come from Fannie Mae's Selling Guide, because it's public. Your loan may follow a different guide. The DTI limits, occupancy types, the 85% investment LTV, and the reserve rules are all Fannie Mae sections, checked on September 25, 2026.

The new short-term rental section, B3-3.8-03, is the one to treat with care. We confirmed the section exists and when it takes effect from the September 2026 announcement. We could not read the full text. So the lesson gives you a conditional version and asks your lender to confirm the rest.

The CFPB pages cover comparing loan offers, the APR, the Loan Estimate, and the business-purpose rule. Kiavi's DSCR page is here as one lender's example, not a recommendation. The lesson's source list also includes Fannie Mae B2-2-03 and the CFPB APR and Loan Estimate explainers.

All Cedar Ridge figures are assumptions from our running example.
